summary: Provides guidelines and procedures for defining, registering and evaluating new interface types (ifType values) and tunnel types in the IANA registry. The registry predated IANA Considerations sections and YANG modules, which caused some confusion that this document clears up. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A big list names all the kinds of network connections. This document gives the rules for adding new kinds to the list so everyone does it the same way and nobody gets confused.

questions: how to register a new iftype
how are tunnel types registered with iana
what is expert review in iana
are yang and mib iftype registries separate
subtitle: The rules for adding new interface types and tunnel types to the IANA registries, now independent of MIB or YANG.

tldr.problem: The IANA ifType registry predated IANA Considerations sections and YANG modules, so confusion arose about whether MIB and YANG forms were separate registries, how to ask for values, and how to handle sub-layers and transmission numbers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states that ifType and tunnelType values are independent of any data model, treats the MIB and YANG modules as extra formats of one registry, adds a validation step and registration templates, and assigns a transmission number alongside each new ifType.
tldr.outcome: Registrants and the designated expert now have written guidance for both registries. The RFC updates RFC 2863.

today: RFC 8892 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2863. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How the Registries Grew
sections.content:
The IANA IfType-MIB, the list of interface type (ifType) values, was first defined in RFC 1573 together with the Interfaces Group MIB. The IF-MIB was later updated in RFC 2863, but that RFC no longer contains the IANA IfType-MIB, which IANA maintains separately. RFC 7224 created an initial IANA Interface Type YANG module, also now maintained by IANA.

The RFC stresses that assigning and using ifType values is not tied to MIB modules or any other management mechanism. A value can appear in a MIB or YANG object, in a unique identifier such as an OID, or simply in a local API or UI. Tunnel types came from the TUNNEL-MIB in RFC 2667 (now obsoleted by RFC 4087), and their assignment policy was defined to be identical to that for ifTypes.
sections.eli5: The list of connection types started inside one particular kind of document, but the list is useful on its own. This RFC says so clearly.

sections.title: The Problems Being Fixed
sections.content:
The RFC lists six problems:

  • Original guidance was worded for MIB modules, which confused YANG users.
  • The use of sub-layers and sub-types was not well understood.
  • Because the registries are retrievable as MIB and YANG modules, people wondered whether each was a separate registry.
  • No process step checked that the MIB and YANG formats stayed syntactically correct, and errors broke tools.
  • Documents said to request values by email even though a web form exists.
  • Transmission values were usually allocated with ifTypes, but there was no guidance on whether to request one.
sections.eli5: People were confused about six things: which rules applied, how to stack connection types, whether there were several lists or one, how to check the list was not broken, where to send requests, and an extra number nobody knew whether to ask for.

sections.title: Sub-layers, Sub-types and Reuse
sections.content:
When several sub-layers sit below the network layer, each can have its own row in the ifTable with its own ifType, and the ifStackTable records how they multiplex. A request involving multiple sub-layers MUST include or reference a discussion of the multiplexing relationships, ideally with a diagram. A sub-layer is generally used when the relationship is dynamic or involves multiplexing. A sub-type fits when neither is true but one type is conceptually a subclass of another. The tunnel(131) ifType, for instance, defines sub-types called tunnelTypes.

Definers should reuse an existing value when it easily meets the modeling and functional needs, so existing tools keep working. They should take a new value when key aspects such as the header format or the link model differ significantly. Two examples from the text: many Ethernet flavors once had separate ifType values, and RFC 3635 deprecated all but ethernetCsmacd(6). Teredo got its own tunnelType in RFC 4087 because it differs from the older udp(8) tunnel type, for example in not supporting multicast or broadcast encapsulation.
sections.eli5: If a new gadget is basically the same as an old one, use the old label. If it works quite differently, give it a new label so tools do not get mixed up.

sections.title: Registration Procedure
sections.content:
The IANA policy is Expert Review for both ifTypes and tunnelTypes. The designated expert raises concerns about wider implications but cannot override properly reached IETF or working group consensus.

A registrant MUST check the registry for an existing entry that would do, check the name is not already taken, prepare a request using the template, and submit it to iana@iana.org or, for an ifType, through a web form. IANA checks completeness, asks the expert to review, and once approved updates the registry and its MIB and YANG formats. IANA should verify that the updated MIB and YANG formats are syntactically correct before publishing. If the expert declines, the registrant can resubmit, or the IESG can override the expert under RFC 8126.

The registry is available in several formats. The MIB and YANG modules are just additional formats, not separate registries, and the same values are always in all of them.
sections.eli5: You check the list, fill in the form, and an expert looks it over. Then the list is updated, and a check makes sure the copies in different file types still work.

sections.title: The Registration Templates
sections.content:
Both templates require a label, a name, a description of proposed use, and a reference such as a document link. A label must be letters and digits, at most 64 characters, starting with a lowercase letter, with no hyphens (labels over 32 characters are not recommended). An optional field is left for extra comments.

The description MUST answer four questions: how IP would run over the type, whether another sub-layer would sit between it and IP, whether it would be vendor specific or proprietary (if so the label MUST start with a string showing that, such as the company acronym), and whether it would require or allow vendor-specific extensions. Before this RFC there was no form for tunnelType; this document supplies one.
sections.eli5: The form asks for a short name, a longer description, and a link to the full details. It also asks simple questions, like whether the new thing belongs to one company.

sections.title: Transmission Numbers and IANA Actions
sections.content:
From now on, an ifType value and a transmission number with the same value are assigned at the same time. The RFC gives reasons: it saves a later request and second expert review, the transmission number space is not scarce, the expert need not review transmission numbers per request, and no recorded case shows that using the same value caused problems. IANA's own note still warns that implementors must not assume a relationship between ifType values and transmission subtree OIDs.

IANA is also asked to relabel the MIB and YANG module entries as formats of the registries, add an 'Interface Parameters' category covering the ifType, tunnelType and Transmission Number registries, and replace the YANG pages with the module content. Some actions were deferred until IANA migrates to a new platform. The document itself has been added as a reference in the affected registries and modules.
sections.eli5: When a new connection type gets a number, it also gets the same number on a second, related list, so nobody has to ask twice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC introduces no technology or protocol, so it says there are no security issues for the document itself. For MIB and YANG modules that expose these values, it points to Section 9 of RFC 2863, Section 6 of RFC 4087 and Section 3 of RFC 8675.
sections.eli5: This is only a rulebook for a list, so it adds no new safety worries.
